title: A Time to Weep and a Time to Love
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Written in the wake of the Uvalde school shooting, Dave reflects on the faces and stories of the victims, including two teacher colleagues, and on the culture of self-interested power-seeking he believes underlies such violence. Drawing on the Golden Rule's near-universal presence across world religious and philosophical traditions, he argues that neighbor-love, not political power, is the only path that has ever produced lasting social change, citing Dr. King, Gandhi, and Liberian president Ellen Johnson Sirleaf as examples. He uses a satellite-and-gravity analogy to describe how sustained love, backed by real initial effort, functions like a partnership with a law of physical reality rather than a fight against it. The piece is explicitly unfinished; Dave stops mid-argument, before reaching practical application, but chose to publish it anyway because it was on his heart.
points: Frames the Golden Rule not as one ethical teaching among many but as a "law" — a description of how reality functions, akin to gravity — because it recurs independently across a dozen unrelated religious and philosophical traditions spanning millennia.

Argues that political power and neighbor-love are fundamentally different fuels: power-seeking, even for good causes, tends to erode love over time, while sustained love-seeking eventually yields the power to shift a culture.

Uses the modern example of satellites — a large one-time energy investment plus alignment with gravity producing "free" ongoing motion — as an analogy for how sustained love becomes exponentially more powerful than direct pursuit of political power.

Cites Dr. King's neighbor-love dismantling Jim Crow, Gandhi's satyagraha humbling the British empire, and Ellen Johnson Sirleaf's reconciliation work in Liberia as cases where love-based movements, initially dismissed as "weak" or "passive," produced outsized and lasting change.
quotes: I typically try to not to dwell on tragedies like this; a soul handles only so much sorrow before it numbs, and ours is a time awash in cause for sorrow.
First: ours is a culture opposed to the dignity of the human soul. Instead of dignity, we obsess on power and self.
Because power isn't the master move; love is. Seek power, and with time even the best intentions lack in love. But seek love, and given enough time you'll have the power to shift a culture.
Love — that is, the earnest seeking of another's good — is the surest and most practical path to healing a culture and the souls within it.
Here's my answer to the question preceding this section: The Golden Rule is less a rule than it is a law — a fundamental description of reality.
Dr. King teaches a movement of millions how to neighbor-love, and this neighbor-love dismantles the century-old evil of Jim Crow.
MLK, Gandhi, and Sirleaf didn't obsess over the "sheer evil" of their others; instead, they obsessed on their deep dignity.
First, if you would have strength in this world, you must change your thinking. The person standing on the other side of the debate you're in is a human being wrought with dignity.
